raw_response:
Right now, in Quzhou in mid-April, my wheat is already in the field from last October, so first I have to bring that wheat to harvest, then hurry to put in summer maize. I don’t farm by counting formulas. I do what has held up on my land and what I can still afford if the year turns bad. I have only 22.5 mu, and some people in my house work outside, so I cannot spread money too thin or spend too many days on fussy crops. Wheat and maize stay the backbone because they feed the house and bring steady grain money. Cotton I keep on a few mu because I know it and it can still make money if the year is decent, but I won’t put too much there because it needs more watching and more sprays. Peanut, millet, and mung bean I keep on smaller patches. They spread risk. If one does poorly, maybe another one still gives me something. I have well water, but pumping costs money, so I will irrigate the wheat and the better grain land first, and for millet and mung bean I will be more saving unless the ground gets too dry.

For fertilizer, I would rather not cut too hard. If I save a little money on fertilizer and then the crop turns weak, that hurts more than wasting a bit. But I also cannot throw money everywhere. So on wheat and maize I keep a medium-heavy hand, about like the better farmers nearby, and on millet and mung bean I keep it light. I use simple timing: some before planting, some later if the crop shows it needs feeding. Labor-wise, I lean on family first and only hire a little when the wheat harvest and maize sowing bump together too tight.
